text: A package can decompress to far more than its own size, so opening watches the device itself, not the package. As it writes a file, and before each file inside a folder (counted at its full size, at least one disk block), the app checks the free space where it writes; it stops with “Not enough space” before less than 500 MiB or 5% of the volume, whichever is smaller, would be left, and removes everything it wrote for that package. A note is opened in memory: in the new format its trailer and both signatures are checked before any of it is decompressed, and in every format the app checks free memory as the decompressed note grows and stops with “Not enough memory” before the note, and the copy shown on screen, would leave less than 256 MiB (on iPhone and iPad, the memory iOS allows the app); the memory the note grew out of is wiped. The free space is read again after at most 64 MiB written, so the margin holds to within about that much, and it does not cover another app filling the disk at the same moment; on a device that cannot report its free space or memory, nothing is refused. These margins are the same for every package and depend only on the device: there is no limit on the size of a file, folder or note, and one of any size opens on a device with room for it.

text: AES-GCM is the most widely implemented cipher of its kind, fast on every platform the app runs on, and it checks its own output: every encrypted message carries a 16-byte tag, and any change to the encrypted bytes or to the extra data bound to them (the associated data) makes decryption fail. The 256-bit key leaves a wide margin, including against a quantum computer running Grover’s search, the best known quantum attack on ciphers like AES.

text: Android has no equivalent of the iOS data protection class that iPhone uses for the app’s files. On an Android phone that is locked but has been unlocked since its last restart, an attacker who can get past Android’s own app separation (a rooted or exploited phone) can read the app’s files. The packages, the identity blob and the contact store are still encrypted by the app and need the person’s keys or password. The DID and display name in the settings file are not, and a file the app has just opened can be read in its private folder until the app empties it (when the decrypt window closes, after the file is shared or saved, or at the next start). Nothing in the app’s text claims iOS-style data protection for Android.
